newsitem.title: USA: AIDS drugs helping but doubts linger.
newsitem.headline: AIDS drugs helping but doubts linger.

text.p: Scientists emerged from a major AIDS conference here confident new therapies are helping patients but seeming less hopeful about prospects of a cure.

"This is a period of sobriety, after the intoxication of Vancouver," said Dr. Douglas Dieterich of New York University, referring to the hopes that soared last July at a conference in Vancouver, where speculation on about a cure was rampant.
The 4th Conference on Retrovirals that ended on Sunday left researchers with a more cautious view of the future.

More than 30 million people have been infected worldwide, and only a "tiny, and only a "tiny, tiny, tiny" minority have access to state-of-the-art therapies, said Peter Piot of the United Nations AIDS programme.

Some researchers at the conference still spoke of possibly eradicating the HIV virus that causes AIDS in a small group of patients who entered a carefully controlled experiment shortly after their initial infection. But they were not talking about a cure for most patients in the near future.
"I personally don't think it (a cure) will work in most patients," said Dr. Robert Schooley of the University of Colorado in Denver. "We have to be realistic."

Study after study illustrated that the new drugs are helping most patients who have access to the costly medications -- not easy in rich countries and virtually impossible in the poor ones that harbour 90 percent of the world's AIDS infections.
A consensus is emerging that patients should be treated early, before the virus shatters the immune system.
"The goal is complete suppression (of the virus) as quickly as possible," said conference chairman Dr. Douglas Richman of the University of California at San Diego.

No one has reliable estimates of how many respond to the new drugs and anecdotal reports vary widely. But empty beds in many AIDS wards tell as much as any statistical analysis about the restoration of hope and prolongation of life.
"After Vancouver, there was a quota of undue optimism," said Dr. Julio Montaner, of the Canadian HIV Trials Network.
"But very major progress has been made, beyond our original expectations. This is a reality, it's not a petri dish," added Montanar, who tracks hundreds of patients.
The problem is that no one can be confident these drugs will work indefinitely, without engendering resistance.

And the drugs do not help everyone. Some patients cannot tolerate the side effects. Some cannot adhere to the intricate regimen involving dozens of pills. Some have had their options limited by past failed therapies. And some are just too sick.
Little is known about how to treat babies and children with AIDS, although some early data was presented that should lead to better pediatric treatment guidelines.

University of Massachusetts at Worcester researcher Katherine Luzuriaga said the virus was suppressed to undetectable levels in a set of twins after 18 months but the drugs did not work as well in six other babies she studied.
